newsitem.title: INDIA: India sees little chance of fresh wheat purchases.
newsitem.headline: India sees little chance of fresh wheat purchases.

text.p: India, bucked by a good wheat crop, timely imports and good rainfall, has comfortable foodgrain stocks and is unlikely to scout for more imports this fiscal year, traders and analysts said on Thursday.
They said India would not need more wheat imports in 1997/98 (April-March) because domestic prices had substantially fallen amid good market arrivals and sufficient stocks with farmers.
"We will not need any more wheat (imports) in 1997/98," Anil Sharma, an agriculture economist at the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) told Reuters.
An U.S. Agriculture Department official said in Washington on Wednesday that India would need to import an additional 1.0 to 2.0 million tonnes later this year.

"For now, they seemed to have filled their needs--at least for the next few months," Thomas Pomeroy, U.S. agricultural counselor in New Delhi told Reuters. "There's a possibility they might buy a million or two more tonnes, but I don't think they're going to do it for several months."
Prem Garg, a leading Delhi foodgrains exporter said: "I don't believe it is possible. The government has already said that they have heavy stocks and farmers too have good wheat stocks."

B.K. Taimini, the seniormost civil servant in the Food Ministry said on Wednesday that India had bought 9.25 million tonnes of wheat from farmers for sale in the 1997/98 marketing season against 8.2 million tonnes in the previous season.

He said as of October 1, 1997 India would have much higher rice stocks than the buffer norms of six million tonnes and on April 1, 1998, India would have wheat stocks well above the required 3.7 million tonnes.
Taimini said India had put on hold the purchase of one million tonnes of wheat out of two million it was authorised to import during the 1997/98 year.
Earlier this year, India bought 2.7 million tonnes of wheat from Australia, Canada and Argentina.

The Indian government in June forecast 1996/97 (July-June) wheat output at 68.71 million tonnes, up from 62.62 million in the previous crop year. It expects overall foodgrains production in 1996/97 to total 198.17 million tonnes compared with 185.04 million in the previous season.
NCAER's Sharma said while there was no immediate need for imports, the USDA forecast of additional imports might have been based on the anticipation of a fall in the wheat crop next year.
"Maybe they are expecting the Indian 1998/99 wheat crop year to be bad," said Sharma. "Maybe they have discounted for a drought year."
Wheat sowing in India begins in January and wheat is marketed between April and June.
Sharma said the monsoon, which usually lasts from June through September, had been good so far this year although there was a need to look at its distribution by region.
"But 80 percent of the wheat cultivated in India is under irrigated land," Sharma said.
O.P. Mangal, vice president of the Space Group, another foodgrain exporter, said India would not need any additional wheat imports in 1997/98.
"The United States also needs some markets so they want to keep some mental pressure on other importers to maintain their prices," said Mangal.
He said India's wheat crop was expected to be much better than anticipated and the rice crop too was forecast to be very good.

Mulraj Tanna, a Bombay foodgrains exporter, said it was very difficult to predict what the country would need in 1998. "We have to look at the final stock position and assess how much the states were lifting," he said.
